1 & 4. Extreme violence, with the use of weapons/machete towards members of the public, specifically males whom he perceives are a threat/ to himself or others  - and particularly when under the influence of drugs/alcohol and in the company of peers/negative influences. Members of the public are considered to be at risk of physical harm, threats of violence and intimidation when Mr Lee is under the fluence of alcohol and/or drugs (cocaine). This is coupled with his subsequent feelings of  paranoia which increases the risk of Mr Lee becoming violent. In addition, witnesses of such violence would be harmed emotionally and psychologically.

2. I have considered risk to unknown females with regard to the indecent assault in 2001, however it is my professional assessment that due to the offence being 16 years ago, and no further similar offences since that time, Mr Lee is not considered a risk of sexual harm to adult females. In addition, Mr Lee has been in a stable relationship with the same partner for a number of years and therefore viewed as a protective factor.

3 & 5.  Should Mr Lee be under the influence and drive, he poses a risk to the wider public in terms of road users and pedestrians should he lose control of the car or if his reactions are impaired.  If his son was in the car, then he is also potentially at risk of physical, emotional and psychological harm.
roshSummary.riskIncreaseFactors:
In accordance with the OGRS 3 scores, Mr Lee is assessed as a high risk of re-offending and his OVP scores place him at medium risk of violent offending. Clinical assessment places him as posing a medium risk of serious harm in light of his offending history, and the index offence of extreme violence.  There is also concern in relation to index offence should he continue to drive whilst under the influence of substances.  

The risk is likely to be at its greatest when Mr Lee is under the influence of alcohol and/or drugs and whilst taking medication. When Mr Lee feels aggrieved or becomes involved in an altercation that involves either himself or others. When he feels threatened, confronted, and intimidated. Any impairment to his reactions when driving could result in erratic driving or crash which may or may not injure himself and also members of the public or family.  

The likelihood of Mr Lee committing further harm is not considered to be immediate as more drug testing is required. When in the community his risk is assessed as medium given his violent  actions, the impact of any future offending could be very serious. Whilst there has been some improvement noted since release, due to recall and further offences, more work and assessment is needed around Mr Lee's thinking and attitude.
roshSummary.riskMitigationFactors:
Employment, reduction in use of alcohol use, abstinence from drugs, engagement/compliance with Probation, improved thinking and behaviourial skills, increased understanding of the impact drugs/alcohol can have on behaviour and maturation.

Factors that will help to reduce risk also include the following:

If Mr Lee remains offence free during his licence period. If he continues to remain drug and alcohol free and access appropriate support via 'We Are With You' re recent cocaine use. If Mr Lee can evidence a change in attitudes in respect of violence. Maintains emotional stability, can accesss support via his GP regarding his ADHD, and access mental health services if needed. Continues to undertake work that will consolidate learning gained in custody via PIPE and programmes completed during his sentence. This will include controlling his aggression and violence and victim empathy. Continuing to achieve a positive work / home balance. Ongoing constructive contact with supportive friends and family.

- Increased reporting to be considered at times of crisis, to enable increased monitoring but also increased support to be offered
- His partner is fully aware of his history of offending.
- Maintained abstinence as by his own admission this impairs his  decision making and consequential thinking
- Drug testing to enable robust monitoring of lifestyle / alcohol use
- Mr Lee continuing to access the support of his GP in respect of emotional well-being, to ensure he has appropriate ongoing treatment and a robust support network should mood dip
- Mr Lee will be subject to recall if a suggestion that risk is becoming unmanageable

offenceAnalysis:
On 12.10.2014 at the Clifton Arms Public House, Clifton Road L6, Mr Lee unlawfully and maliciously wounded Liam Thompson with intent to do him grievous bodily harm, section 18 offence against a person.
Mr Lee used a machete type blade to strike Liam Thompson on the shoulder and the hand. Injuries sustained by the victim resulted in his right ring finger being severed. The finger was only attached to his hand by a small piece of skin. Further injuries included a deep laceration across the right palm, and a deep laceration to his right shoulder approximately 2-3 inches long.
Since the revocation request on 22.10.2014 I have visited Mr Lee on one occasion on Wednesday 4th November 2014 at HMP Liverpool and have had sight of the Crown Prosecution Service documentation.
During interview with Mr Lee, he explained that since his release from prison on 10/06/2014 he had been abstinent from alcohol and cocaine up until two days prior to the offence. 
Mr Lee reported that on Friday 10/10/14 he had been invited to the Clifton Arms Pub for a leaving party for the son of the owner, stating he arrived with his girlfriend at approximately 7pm where he stayed drinking Jack Daniels and using cocaine until approximately 11am the following morning. He explained the pub had remained open to the guests throughout the night which encouraged him to stay there as he was ‘getting on’ with everyone and he liked the feelings he got from drinking and taking cocaine. 
Mr Lee explained how on Saturday 11/10/2014 he went home to get some rest, leaving friends at the pub. He claims he was invited out again, Saturday night to Liverpool city centre and stated he began drinking and taking cocaine once more from approximately 9pm right through into the afternoon of Sunday 12/10/2014 when the offence took place.


It is clear that Mr Lee’s behaviour on the days running up to the offence were fuelled by excessive alcohol and drug abuse, combined with his own mental health state of paranoia, which he was taking medication for. He accepts that his triggers for violent behaviour are a combination of these with situations whereby he feels threatened and confronted therefore placed Mr Lee at an imminent risk of causing serious harm.

whatLedToRecall:
Mr Lee has failed to notify the supervising officer as to where he is permanently residing.  There have been concerns around his behaviour and display of superficial compliance.  Information was received from Police following a callout out to the address on 14th April when Mr Lee was spotted climbing into the property via a back window.  When Police arrived he was found in the kitchen, he stated he did not have keys.  Officers noted he appeared under the influence of substances and believed he was not residing there.  A social services MARF was submitted and closed, with conflicting information as to his poermanent residence.  Due to concerns of where Mr Lee was residing due to conflicting information provided, a different address appeared on his GP fit notes, an unannounced home visit was conducted on 27th May 2026,  Upon arrival Mr Lee was not present as confirmed during the visit whilst his partner was present. The PP then visited the address on the fit note to find this was under construction and no residents present.  

Mr Lee failed to attend his office appointment at 16:30 hours and advised that he had been at home all day with vomiting bug, however he was not present as confirmed by the Home visit.   Prior to the recall application, there have been concerns around Mr Lee’s overall compliance, whilst subject to licence he has been subject to a suspended sentence order and community order for driving under the influence of drugs.  Probation have submitted a variation of EDS licence to PPCS for addition of alcohol abstinence tag  as a prevention to recall and he is due to appear before the Magistrates on Friday 29th May for breach of unpaid work.  There have been positive tests for both cocaine and cannabis and by his own admission he has relapsed also to alcohol use.  These factors are a direct risk escalation triggers and were present in the commission of the EDS index offence.  

Mr Lee has been afforded a great deal of flexibility and chances to improve,  due to the seriousness of his EDS licence, however, given new information and clear deterioration, plus superficial compliance, it is deemed that he is no longer manageable and poses a risk in the community.  Thus recall action has been taken.
